subsection: 3. Case study: the elections of 1885 and 1886 — issues and outcomes

notes.h: Background: Home Rule, Parnell and British politics before 1885
notes.b: The two elections of 1885 and 1886 were fought over one question, Home Rule. To follow them you need to know what Home Rule meant, who Parnell was by 1885 and how British government worked.
points: Home Rule was the demand for an Irish parliament in Dublin to handle domestic affairs, while Ireland stayed inside the Union of 1800 (the Acts of Union joining Ireland to Great Britain). It is not separatism, which means full independence.
Butt's Home Rule League (1873) had made Home Rule a parliamentary movement, pursued by votes at Westminster rather than by force.

By 1885 Charles Stewart Parnell had risen fast: Land League president (1879), chairman of the Irish Parliamentary Party (1880), imprisoned in Kilmainham Gaol (October 1881 to May 1882) and founder of the Irish National League (1882), which replaced the banned Land League.

Gladstone's Liberal government (1880-85) answered the Land War (the campaign by tenant farmers against landlords) with coercion, meaning emergency laws such as the Coercion Act of 1881 and the Crimes Act of 1882. Nationalists never forgave this.
The Phoenix Park murders of 6 May 1882 (Lord Frederick Cavendish and Thomas Burke) left Liberals and nationalists with a bitter legacy, which is why co-operation between them in 1885 was surprising.

In Britain the Liberals (led by W.E. Gladstone) and the Conservatives (led by Lord Salisbury) alternated in power. A government needs a majority of seats in the Commons, and the House of Lords could still reject a bill.
Lord Hartington led the Whig wing of the Liberals, the cautious, landowning side, so he was likely to resist radical change such as Home Rule.

Ulster had a Protestant majority in the north-east, above all Belfast and east Ulster, and a Catholic nationalist majority in the south and west of the province. Unionists wanted to keep the Union; nationalists wanted Home Rule.
notes.tip: Keep Home Rule (a parliament within the Union) apart from separatism (full independence). Examiners reward answers that state the issue precisely before giving the events.

notes.h: Background: the new electorate and constituencies (1884-1885)
notes.b: Two Acts rewrote the electoral map just before the 1885 election, and Parnell's organised party was the main beneficiary. This was a step towards democracy, which means government through elected representatives, though here for men only.
points: The Representation of the People Act 1884 (the Third Reform Act) gave the vote to male householders and lodgers in the counties on the same terms as the boroughs (towns), ending the old gap between town and country. It applied to Ireland, and women were still excluded.
In Ireland the electorate rose from about 220,000 to about 740,000, more than tripling, because the new voters were mostly small farmers and agricultural labourers (estimates vary a little).

The Redistribution of Seats Act 1885 abolished many small boroughs and made most constituencies single-member, though a few, such as Cork City and Dublin University, stayed two-member. Ireland kept its 103 seats.
Single-member rural seats favoured a party organised in every parish, and the Irish National League had branches across the country, run by local committees and often led by priests.

Candidates were chosen at constituency conventions, where the clergy were influential. From 1884 each candidate had to take the pledge, an undertaking to sit, act and vote with the Irish Party, so the party could vote as a bloc.
Voting stayed secret under the Ballot Act of 1872, so tenants could vote against their landlords without fear of eviction.
The Catholic hierarchy, led by William Walsh, Archbishop of Dublin, and Thomas Croke, Archbishop of Cashel, backed the party in return for its support on Catholic education.
notes.tip: Do not mix up the two Acts: the Third Reform Act (1884) was about the vote, the Redistribution of Seats Act (1885) was about the constituencies. The electorate more than tripled, and you should say who the new voters were.

notes.h: Parnell's balance-of-power strategy and the Maamtrasna alliance (1884-1885)
notes.b: Parnell's aim was to hold the balance of power, meaning a smaller party whose votes decide which larger party governs. He would bargain with both British parties and give support to whichever offered more on Home Rule.
points: At Cork on 21 January 1885 Parnell declared that no man had the right to fix the boundary to the march of a nation. This was a demand for Home Rule as a national claim, not a limited local parliament.

In 1884 Conservatives such as Lord Randolph Churchill joined the Irish MPs in attacking the Liberal Lord Lieutenant, Earl Spencer (Lord Lieutenant 1882-85), over the Maamtrasna murders of August 1882.
At Maamtrasna, Myles Joyce was hanged in December 1882 despite doubts about his guilt, so nationalists used the case as a symbol of the injustice of Liberal coercion.
That common cause is called the Maamtrasna alliance, and it opened the way to co-operation between Parnell and the Conservatives, though the two sides wanted different things.

On 9 June 1885 the Irish Party voted with the Conservatives on an amendment to Gladstone's budget and brought down his government. Lord Salisbury formed a minority Conservative ministry, one that could survive only while others did not combine against it.
notes.tip: Cause and effect questions ask how Parnell used the balance of power. Name the date (9 June 1885) and the event, not just the idea.

notes.h: Bargaining with both parties: Carnarvon, Chamberlain and the manifesto (1885)
notes.b: With Salisbury in office, Parnell tested what each side would give. Home Rule emerged as the only demand that satisfied him.
points: Lord Carnarvon, Salisbury's Lord Lieutenant of Ireland (a Conservative), met Parnell secretly in London in August 1885. The Crimes Act was allowed to lapse, which removed coercion, a major grievance.
The Ashbourne Act (August 1885) provided state loans for tenant purchase, so that tenants could buy their land from landlords. It was part of the Conservatives' offer.

Joseph Chamberlain, a Liberal radical, proposed an elected Central Board for Ireland, discussed through Captain William O'Shea. Parnell and Gladstone's Cabinet both rejected it in 1885, which left Home Rule as the demand.
At Arklow in October 1885 Parnell set out a demand for a legislature with control of Irish domestic affairs, and he stressed that Ireland would not be satisfied with less.
Parnell's manifesto of 21 November 1885 told Irish voters in Britain to vote against Liberal candidates, because of Liberal coercion in 1881-82. This was reversed after the Hawarden Kite.
notes.tip: Do not confuse Carnarvon (Conservative Lord Lieutenant), Spencer (Liberal Lord Lieutenant) and Morley (Chief Secretary, 1886). Salisbury's first government (June 1885 to January 1886) is not his second (July 1886 onwards).

notes.b: The election produced a hung Parliament, one in which no party has an overall majority, with the Irish Party holding the balance. It also split Ireland along religious and regional lines.
points: Polling ran from late November to mid-December 1885. The Irish Party won 85 of the 103 Irish seats, plus T.P. O'Connor at Liverpool Scotland, giving 86 MPs in all.
Outside Ulster the only seats the party did not win were the two for Dublin University. The party swept the south and west (85 = 17 in Ulster + 68 elsewhere).
In Ulster the party won 17 of 33 seats, in the Catholic-majority districts of the south and west of the province. Unionists won the rest, strongest in the east of Ulster.
In Great Britain the Liberals won about 335 seats, the Conservatives about 249 and the Irish Party 86, in a House of 670 (counts vary slightly).
Neither big party could govern without the Irish: the Irish Party plus the Conservatives could equal the Liberals, and Irish votes could decide who governed. Parnell held the balance of power.
The Irish vote in British cities, especially Liverpool, may have helped Conservative candidates in some constituencies after the manifesto, though its effect is hard to measure.

Nationalists and Liberals saw the result as a national mandate, a clear verdict that Ireland, outside Protestant Ulster, wanted Home Rule. Unionists and Conservatives replied that two Irelands had voted.
notes.tip: If asked why the Irish Party won 85 seats, give the new voters, the National League organisation, the clergy and the pledge. Ulster is the exception to explain: 17 of 33 seats, in the Catholic districts.

notes.h: The Hawarden Kite and Gladstone's conversion (December 1885 to March 1886)
notes.b: Gladstone moved to Home Rule within weeks of the election and took office again in February 1886. His move cost him part of his own party.
points: On 17 December 1885 newspapers published the Hawarden Kite, a leak by Gladstone's son Herbert reporting that Gladstone favoured Home Rule. Hawarden, in Flintshire, was Gladstone's home, and a kite is a trial balloon to test opinion.

Salisbury's ministry was defeated on 26 January 1886 on an amendment about allotments for labourers (Jesse Collings), with the Irish voting against it. Gladstone formed his third ministry in February 1886, with John Morley as Chief Secretary for Ireland.

Joseph Chamberlain joined the Cabinet but resigned in March 1886, along with Sir George Trevelyan, because they would not accept Home Rule, which showed the Liberals splitting. Lord Hartington declined to serve.
Historians disagree why Gladstone took up Home Rule: genuine conviction after the 1885 result, or tactical manoeuvre to keep the Liberals together, as argued by A.B. Cooke and John Vincent.
notes.tip: Do not confuse the Hawarden Kite (December 1885, a leak) with the First Home Rule Bill (April 1886). Gladstone's second ministry ended in June 1885, his third ran from February to July 1886.

notes.h: The First Home Rule Bill: terms and Parnell's response (April 1886)
notes.b: The Government of Ireland Bill was Gladstone's attempt to give Ireland self-government without breaking up the empire. It reserved to Westminster the matters that made the empire one state.
points: Gladstone introduced the Government of Ireland Bill on 8 April 1886. It would have set up an Irish legislature in Dublin with an executive (government) responsible to it.
The Crown, defence, foreign policy, trade and the customs remained with Westminster, so Ireland would not have been independent.
Ireland was to pay a fixed share, one fifteenth, of imperial expenditure. The Irish members would no longer sit at Westminster, which meant Ireland would have no voice in imperial decisions.
The Irish legislature was to have two orders, designed to reassure Protestants and property owners, and it was forbidden to establish or endow any religion.
A companion Land Purchase Bill would have offered loans to buy out the landlords. It was unpopular in Britain and was not proceeded with, which weakened the main bill.
Parnell accepted the bill as a basis for a settlement, because it granted an Irish legislature, though he objected to its financial terms.
notes.tip: Ordinary Level questions on a document ask who introduced the bill and what its result was: Gladstone, 8 April 1886; defeated in June 1886. Know the terms: what was reserved and what was devolved.

notes.b: The Liberal split, not the Conservatives alone, defeated the First Home Rule Bill. Both sides had set out their arguments during weeks of debate.
points: The bill was debated for several weeks in April-June 1886, and the second reading was defeated in the early hours of 8 June 1886 by 341 votes to 311, a majority of 30.
About 93 Liberals, led by Hartington and Chamberlain, voted with the Conservatives against the bill. They became the Liberal Unionists, a Liberal group that opposed Home Rule and kept the Union.
John Bright, the veteran radical, also opposed the bill. Chamberlain argued that it would break up the empire and treat Ulster Protestants unfairly.
Conservatives such as Lord Randolph Churchill argued that Home Rule meant separation and the loss of the Protestant minority's rights.
Gladstone's supporters argued that coercion had failed, that Ireland's verdict was clear and that Home Rule would give Ireland a settled government and reconcile it to the Crown.
In his closing speech on 7 June 1886 Gladstone said Ireland stood at your bar, expectant, hopeful, almost suppliant, an appeal to conscience made before the vote.
After the defeat Gladstone dissolved Parliament in late June 1886 and called a general election.
notes.tip: If asked why the bill failed, the strong answer is the Liberal split: about 93 Liberals voted against, not just the Conservatives. Give 341 to 311 and a majority of 30.

notes.h: Unionist mobilisation: the Orange card and the Belfast riots
notes.b: The crisis of 1886 created organised unionism in Ulster and in the south. Unionists feared an Irish parliament would be a Catholic parliament.
points: In a letter of February 1886 Lord Randolph Churchill wrote that the Orange card was the one to play against Home Rule, meaning an appeal to Ulster Protestants (the Orange Order is their loyalist society). He spoke at the Ulster Hall, Belfast, on 22 February 1886.
The phrase Ulster will fight and Ulster will be right is associated with Churchill in 1886, and unionists used it as a slogan for decades.
The Irish Loyal and Patriotic Union, formed in 1885 by southern unionists, mainly landlords and professionals, who had property to lose, organised opposition to Home Rule.
Ulster Protestants established a Loyalist Anti-Repeal organisation in 1886 (repeal meaning undoing the Union), and the Orange Order grew sharply.
The Belfast riots began in early June 1886, with the bill's defeat in prospect, and lasted into September. About 30 or more people were killed and many injured (estimates vary).
The violence deepened sectarian division, and both sides used it as evidence. Nationalists blamed unionist mobs and the Orange Order; unionists blamed Home Rule agitation.
notes.tip: Do not confuse the Irish Loyal and Patriotic Union (southern unionists, 1885) with the later Ulster Unionist Council and UVF. For the riots, give the scale with a hedge and both interpretations.

notes.h: The July 1886 election and its outcomes
notes.b: The voters rejected Gladstone, and the Conservatives governed for most of the next twenty years. The elections left a changed political landscape.
points: In July 1886 the Conservatives and Liberal Unionists won a combined majority of over 100 over the Gladstonian Liberals and the Irish Party.
Salisbury formed his second government in July 1886, which survived because it was supported by the Liberal Unionists, who entered a coalition with the Conservatives in 1895.
The Irish Party again won about 85 seats, so the nationalist case was undiminished.

Home Rule was now the policy of the Liberal Party. The Liberal-Nationalist alliance became the central fact of Irish parliamentary politics until 1914, because Home Rule now depended on Liberal votes.
Home Rule could pass only when the Liberals had a majority able to overcome the Lords, which was not achieved until the Parliament Act of 1911, because the Liberal split had weakened them.
Unionism became a lasting organised force in Ireland and Britain, and this was the origin of the Ulster question, the problem of Protestant Ulster's opposition to Home Rule.
Parnell was at the height of his power, with a disciplined party and a Liberal ally. The Pigott forgeries and the O'Shea divorce came next.
notes.tip: Strong essays name the outcomes: Liberal split, Conservative government, Liberal-Nationalist alliance and organised unionism, then give a judgement. The First Home Rule Bill (1886) is not the Second (1893) or the Third (1912).

notes.h: Key personality: Charles Stewart Parnell (role in the 1885-1886 elections)
notes.b: Parnell was the central figure in the case study. He made the Irish Party decisive and tied Home Rule to the Liberals.
points: Parnell was born in 1846 at Avondale, Co. Wicklow, a Protestant landowner and an MP from 1875, and leader of the Irish Party.
He built the party machine, using the National League, the pledge and conventions, so that the party could deliver its votes as a bloc.
He bargained with Carnarvon in 1885 and issued the manifesto against the Liberals, then supported Gladstone, showing tactical skill in keeping both British parties guessing.
In the Galway by-election of February 1886 he imposed Captain O'Shea on the party against Tim Healy's objections, which showed his control but sowed resentment.
He was a participant who led the campaigns and the bargaining, but events also shaped him: he depended on Gladstone surviving, and the Liberal split and unionist backlash limited him.
Nationalist contemporaries saw the 85 seats as a national triumph. Unionists and many Conservatives saw an agitator linked to violence, a reputation The Times later attacked with forged letters.

Examiners ask about his strengths, such as discipline and the pledge, tactics with both parties, balance of power, and appeal to Fenians and constitutionalists. His weaknesses were reliance on a British ally, secrecy about his private life, imposing O'Shea, and aloofness.
F.S.L. Lyons (1977) sees 1885-86 as Parnell's zenith; others note that his strategy depended on Gladstone surviving the Liberal split.
notes.tip: Each strength or weakness needs a date or event, such as the Galway by-election of February 1886 for imposing O'Shea.

notes.h: Views of each side and the kinds of documents
notes.b: Documents on this case study are speeches, newspaper reports and cartoons. Each can be placed by who produced it, when and why.
points: Nationalists (Freeman's Journal, United Ireland) presented the 1885 result as a national verdict and the First Home Rule Bill as a just but limited settlement.
Unionists (Belfast News-Letter, the Irish Loyal and Patriotic Union) presented Home Rule as a threat to the empire, to property and to Protestants.
Gladstone's speeches argued that Home Rule was a moral duty after the failure of coercion; his critics called it a surrender to agitators.
Liberal Unionist speeches, by Chamberlain and Hartington, argued that Irish self-government would endanger the union of the two islands.

Punch, drawn by John Tenniel and others, usually depicted Irish agitators as violent or ape-like, as in The Irish Frankenstein of 1882, and took an anti-Home Rule line. Some Irish and radical papers published pro-Home Rule cartoons.

A cartoon can be placed by its date and symbols: Gladstone as the old man with an axe, Parnell as a tempter or bully, Hibernia (Ireland personified) as a woman, John Bull (Britain personified) as a stout man.

Historians differ on why Gladstone took up Home Rule: conviction after the 1885 result, or tactics to keep the Liberals together, as argued by A.B. Cooke and John Vincent in The Governing Passion (1974).
notes.tip: For a document, say who produced it and when, and what it is for. Criticism: a speech is persuasive and an extract is edited; a cartoon that attacks Home Rule and the Irish is biased.

notes.b: The elections were a triumph for the Irish Party and a defeat for Home Rule. Examiners reward paired judgements.
points: Achievement: the Irish Party won a national mandate, forced Home Rule onto the British agenda and won over a major British party.
Limit: the party could not pass a bill without a British majority, and Gladstone's conversion split the Liberals and put the Conservatives in power.
Achievement: the bill's defeat was narrow, and the Liberal alliance gave nationalists a realistic route to Home Rule.
Limit: the elections showed that Ulster Protestants were opposed, a problem that Parnell's party never answered.
Contemporary nationalists blamed the Liberal Unionists and the House of Commons; contemporary unionists said the vote showed the Union was safe.
Later historians see 1886 as the origin of the Ulster question as well as of the Liberal-Nationalist alliance, which makes it a turning point whatever its immediate failure.
notes.tip: Structure a judgement as achievement against limit, and contemporary against later views, and name a historian such as Lyons.
